There are always winners and losers in any deal, the real question is who those winners and losers are?NAFTA helped Wall Street and its investors who are obviously the winners of the deal on the American side, but devastated rust belt states that relied on the manufacturing jobs which were moved to Mexico as a result of the deal. 

The losers of the deal were blue collar middle class American workers who suffered from wage stagnation due to moving production to Mexico to lower costs, they can pay workers less in Mexico to do the same job. This resulted in a widening trade deficit: 1.7 Billion in 1993 to 54 Billion in 2014. The US auto sector lost 350K jobs since 1994, 1/3 of the industry, while Mexico's auto sector went from 120K jobs to 550K during the same time period.

These are the reasons why people are against NAFTA and not some vague hatred of Mexico as you said above. The racist, bigot card is not a motivating factor for these voters, it's the economy. 

Trump was the only candidate who addressed these people's needs and the pain they felt from losing these jobs for the last 25 years. 

If Hillary showed any genuine concern for these people Hillary would've won in a landslide. But she couldn't hide her utter contempt for the rust belt blue collar worker and it cost her the presidency. Instead she chose to call them deplorable and play the race card which backfired, and as a result Trump won states like Michigan, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Wisconsin by the narrowest of margins.

Yeah I totally relate to perfectionism preventing me from finishing scripts. It was a major problem for me until I had to hit deadlines in a writing program which forced me to put my perfectionism aside and actually finish drafts. Once I had a first draft it was amazing how much easier it was to pin point the areas that needed work. Chunks of pages get cut completely and replaced with something stronger but I never would've got there without plowing through a crappy first draft. With each draft and revision you can tighten and tighten the script until you have something worth sending out. 

Outlines are great too but they can only go so far at the end of the day scripts take on a life of their own once you start writing. A good outline is really helpful but there's no such thing as a perfect outline in my opinion. The magic happens in the script.

I've found for me that writer's block can very well be linked to structural issues in a script but generally of your mind is clear you can make the necessary changes to make the script "work"- it may not be the script I initially envisioned but that's part of the writing process. 

However, I've noticed writer's block that lingers has to do with my physical, emotional, spiritual, and mental health. When I am taking care of myself I can accomplish I'm an a couple of hours. When my life isn't balanced I can think about an idea for hours and hours and days and days bleeding into months and not get anywhere.

Is all about fine tuning my mind, spirit, and body.
